The Black Death. Between 1347 and 1353, a catastrophic pandemic of bubonic plague swept across Eurasia and North Africa, killing an estimated 75 to 200 million people. It arrived in Europe through trade routes, decimating populations by up to 60 percent in some regions and profoundly reshaping medieval society.

The disease was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread primarily by fleas on infected rats. It also transmitted directly between humans in the pneumonic form. The Black Death began in Central Asia and reached Europe via Genoese traders fleeing the Mongol siege of Kaffa in 1347, where some accounts report that plague-infected corpses were catapulted over the city walls.

Across Eurasia, the death toll was staggering. In Europe alone, populations declined by 30 to 60 percent in major cities and trade centers. The disease was characterized by painful swollen lymph nodes called buboes, blackened tissue from gangrene, and rapid death. Most victims died within days of infection.

The pandemic prompted mass migration of survivors and the creation of flagellant movements as people sought divine atonement. Violent pogroms erupted against Jewish communities, who were falsely blamed for the disease. The labor shortages that followed raised wages for surviving workers and contributed significantly to the decline of feudalism across Europe. Contemporary chronicles, including those by Jean de Venette and Giovanni Boccaccio in his Decameron, recorded the social chaos and moral breakdown during the peak years of mortality.
